'''Philip J. Wyatt''' is an American scientist and businessman who is the founder and [[Chairman]] of Wyatt Technology, located in [[Santa Barbara, California]].  He is known for contributions to laser light scattering, more specifically the physics of the [[inverse scattering problem]] and for commercializing analytical methods and instruments involving laser light scattering, which are widely used in academia, industry, and government.

==Early life and education==
Wyatt did undergraduate work at the [[University of Chicago]], (B.A., 1952; B.Sc., 1954), and [[Christ's College, Cambridge]]. He received his M.S. from the [[University of Illinois]] in 1956<ref name="Tretkoff"/> and his Ph.D. from [[Florida State University]] in 1959, where he first worked on the inverse scattering problem.  His Ph.D. work involved the development of a non‑local nuclear model of the scattering of neutrons by nuclei.<ref name="Tretkoff"/>

He was nominated by the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1965 as one of sixteen possible candidates for the first Scientist-Astronaut Selection Program in the United States.<ref name="APS">{{cite web|title=Forum on Industrial & Applied Physics|url=https://www.aps.org/units/fiap/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Philip&last_nm=Wyatt&year=2009|website=APS Physicsa|accessdate=August 26, 2016}}</ref><ref name="SBCC"/>

==Career==
As a graduate student, Wyatt worked at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]]. During the 1960s,  he worked for the [[Aeronutronic]] division of [[Ford Motor Company]], General Research Corporation in Santa Barbara, California, and the defense contractor [[EG&G]].<ref name="APS"/>

Wyatt founded his first company, Science Spectrum, Inc., in 1968.  The company developed several instruments that could be used to study the inverse scattering problem. They applied light-scattering techniques to the detection of [[biological weapons]] and the monitoring of [[food quality]]. These early instruments used a traditional single detector to scan a range of scattering angles.  Shortly before the closure of the company in 1982, Wyatt developed an instrument for [[multi-angle light scattering]] (MALS) in which a glass capillary containing a sample was surrounded by an array of detectors.<ref name="AZO">{{cite web|title=Commercializing Multi-Angle Light Scattering Instruments - An Interview with Philip Wyatt|url=http://www.azom.com/article.aspx?ArticleID=12833|website=AZO Materials|accessdate=August 26, 2016|date = May 20, 2016}}</ref>

Wyatt then founded Wyatt Technology Corporation to develop and sell laser‑based scientific instruments for light scattering and particle size measurement.  His  instruments are used worldwide by universities, government agencies, the biotech industry and pharmaceutical companies.<ref name="Tretkoff"/><ref name="Reisch">{{cite journal|last1=Reisch|first1=Marc S.|title=Instrument Maker Wyatt Charts Its Own Course|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=January 21, 2013|volume=91|issue=3|pages=16–17|doi=10.1021/cen-09103-bus1 |url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/91/i3/Instrument-Maker-Wyatt-Charts-Own.html?h=477274478|accessdate=August 27, 2016|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Wyatt's instruments are used in a wide variety of fields.  Laser particle analysis has been applied to [[wine]] and to [[cleaning products]].<ref name="AZO"/><ref name="Reisch"/> The [[U.S. Government]] has supported work on the identification of bioterrorism threats such as airborne bacteria<ref name="Tretkoff"/> and metabolic poisons or carcinogens in drinking water.<ref name="AZO"/>   Wyatt's instruments are used for [[protein analysis]] by biopharmaceutical companies such as [[Amgen]].<ref name="Reisch"/> They are used for detection of [[Drug residues|drug]] and [[pesticide residues]] in [[meat]], and monitoring for possible [[toxicity]] of [[Zidovudine|AZT]] and [[antineoplastic drugs]] in patients.<ref name="Tretkoff"/> Nobel prize winner [[Robert H. Grubbs]] uses them to study [[polymers]].<ref name="Reisch"/> They are also used to monitor [[smog]] and [[fly ash]], and identify effective [[antibiotics]] to counter [[bacterial infections]].<ref name="Tretkoff"/>

{{blockquote| “Get into a market that is just on the verge of developing. If you’re too early, the company fails. If you’re a little too late, the competitors will eat you alive because  they have much better resources.” Philip J. Wyatt<ref name="Tretkoff"/>}}

Wyatt has published over seventy publications, including books. He has at least ninety domestic and foreign patents related to laser light scattering and other technologies.<ref name="Papers">{{cite web|title=Philip J. Wyatt, Ph.D.|url=http://www.wyatt.com/about/team-wyatt/philip-j-wyatt.html|website=Wyatt Technology|accessdate=August 27, 2016}}</ref>

Wyatt served as the  2012-2013 Chair of the [[American Physical Society]]'s Forum on Industrial and Applied Physics.<ref name="Tretkoff"/> Wyatt also served as the 2018-2019 Chair and 2016-2017 Vice Chair of the American Physical Society’s Group on Instrument and Measurement Science.<ref name="Wyatt">{{cite web|title=Philip J. Wyatt elected Vice-Chair of APS GIMS|url=http://www.wyatt.com/events/news/philip-j.-wyatt-elected-vice-chair-of-aps-gims.html|website=Wyatt Technology|accessdate=August 27, 2016}}</ref>

Wyatt also served on the board of directors of the [[Santa Barbara City College]].<ref name="SBCC">{{cite web|title=SBCC Foundation Board of Directors Philip J. Wyatt, PhD|url=http://www.sbccfoundation.org/sbcc-foundation-board-directors-philip-j-wyatt-phd/|website=SBCC Foundation|date=April 19, 2016}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* 2022, American Physical Society’s George E. Pake Prize, “For pioneering accomplishments and entrepreneurial leadership exemplified by successful global commercialization of laser-based light scattering measurements with multiple applications in biotechnology, analytical chemistry, and nanoparticle characterization.”<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prize Recipient|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm|access-date=October 28, 2021|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref>
* 2009, Inaugural Prize for Industrial Applications of Physics from the American Physical Society “for pioneering developments in the physics of the inverse scattering problem: new application of laser light scattering and the successful sustained commercialization of new related analytical methods and instrumentation.”<ref name="Tretkoff">{{cite journal|last1=Tretkoff|first1=Ernie|title=APS Awards First Industrial Physics Prize to Philip J. Wyatt|journal=APS News|date=2008|volume=11|url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200811/physicsprize.cfm|accessdate=July 26, 2016}}</ref><ref name="LCGC">{{cite news|title=Wyatt CEO receives 2009 prize for Industrial Application of Physics|url=http://www.chromatographyonline.com/wyatt-ceo-receives-2009-prize-industrial-application-physics-1|accessdate=August 26, 2016|work=LCGC|date=December 19, 2008}}</ref>
* 2003, "Graduate of Distinction", college of arts and sciences, Florida State University.<ref name="APS"/>
* Fellow, American Physical Society<ref name="APS"/>
* Fellow, [[Optical Society of America]]<ref name="APS"/>
* Member, [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name="APS"/>
* Member, [[American Society for Microbiology]]<ref name="APS"/>
* Member, [[American Association of Pharmaceutical Scientists]]<ref name="APS"/>
* Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS)<ref name="APS"/>
